**Title:** Similar climates, different interactions: lineage composition shapes the global geography of butterfly–ant associations

**Running title:** Lineages, climate and butterfly–ant interactions

**Draft for co-authors, `r format(Sys.Date(), "%d %B %Y")`.** Every number is computed from the analysis outputs (`code/s01`–`s37`). Main text about 7,100 words; abstract about 300 (Introduction to Discussion, without captions and Table 1); one table and four figures; Supporting Information follows the references.

# Abstract {-}

**Aim:** Lycaenid butterfly larvae interact with ants in four ways, from no association to obligate mutualism and parasitism. We asked whether the global geography of these strategies follows climate or the lineages that each region holds.

**Location:** Global.

**Time period:** Present; climate change since the Last Glacial Maximum.

**Major taxa studied:** Lycaenidae (Lepidoptera).

**Methods:** For `r format(n_class, big.mark = ",")` classified species, we compared climate and lineage as predictors of held-out species, genera, subfamilies and realms, compared regions within shared climate strata and decomposed their obligate faunas, related the spread of genera to obligacy, and tested warmth, dry-season length, water stress, soils, fire and ants given region and lineage and in matched comparisons of related species.

**Results:** Within climate strata shared by the Cape and the Mediterranean Basin, `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_1"))` of the Cape's classified species and `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_2"))` of the Basin's were obligate associates (difference `r pts(std(cb, "difference"))` percentage points, 95% interval `r pts(std(cb, "difference_low"))`–`r pts(std(cb, "difference_high"))`); southern Australia differed less certainly. Lineage predicted the obligacy of held-out species and realms (deviance explained `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))` and `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage"))`) but hardly that of held-out genera; climate models explained at most `r pct(clim_max)`. The southern faunas held more of their subfamilies' obligate genera than a lineage-conserving null predicts. Obligate genera occupied `r num(exp(-spm("Hexagons occupied (log)")), 1)` times fewer hexagons than other genera of similar age and size, but not clearly fewer than their sister clades. Obligate mutualists lived in warmer, more seasonal climates than facultative relatives, but not at matched temperature and biome.

**Main conclusions:** The geography of butterfly–ant interactions follows the lineages each region holds more closely than its climate: similar climates hold different interactions because they hold different genera, and southern faunas hold disproportionately the obligate genera of their subfamilies. Why these lineages became obligate and remained in the south is unresolved.

**Keywords:** ant–butterfly interactions, biogeography, climate, lineage composition, Lycaenidae, Mediterranean-climate regions, mutualism, myrmecophily, parasitism, phylogenetic niche conservatism

# Introduction

Most lycaenid butterflies interact with ants as larvae, and these interactions range from no association, through facultative tending, to obligate mutualism and obligate parasitism of ant colonies (Pierce et al., 2002; Pierce & Dankowicz, 2022). The strategies are distributed very unevenly across the globe. Obligate associates are concentrated in southern Africa and Australia, whereas in the Americas they are rare or absent (Pierce et al., 2002; Fiedler, 2021).

Pierce et al. (2002) noted that obligate associations are more common in the Southern Hemisphere and suggested that this is partly because highly ant-associated lineages make up more of the southern fauna. This suggestion has not been tested against its alternatives, which act at very different timescales. The first concerns present environments. Ants are less active and less abundant in cold climates, and in the Swiss Alps lycaenid species with weaker ant interactions occur in colder places (Pellissier et al., 2012). In seasonally dry, fire-prone biomes, larvae that shelter in ant nests may escape fire, desiccation and food shortage (Cottrell, 1984; Espeland et al., 2023). Old, nutrient-poor landscapes, where plants produce carbohydrates in excess and ants are abundant and dominant, have also been invoked for the Cape and Australia (Orians & Milewski, 2007; Hopper, 2009; Pierce & Dankowicz, 2022). The second concerns the Late Quaternary: regions with little climate change since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) may have allowed specialists that depend on partners to persist (Dynesius & Jansson, 2000; Sandel et al., 2011). The third concerns which lineages reached and persisted in each region; only a few, climatically filtered lineages of blues reached the New World, for example (Vila et al., 2011). If dependence on particular ants also limits how far lineages spread, obligate faunas should be regional, and obligate genera more confined than their relatives.

Separating these explanations is difficult because the strategies are concentrated in few lineages, which also occupy particular climates. An association between climate and the strategies across space can therefore reflect where lineages live rather than what climates favour. We combined a global compilation of lycaenid–ant interactions with occurrence records to map the four strategies, and asked four questions. First, do regions with overlapping measured climatic conditions hold the same strategies? Second, does climate predict the strategies of species, lineages and whole realms that were not used to fit the model, and how does it compare with lineage? Third, are obligate genera more confined than other genera? Fourth, which associations with climate, drought, soils, fire and ants remain once region and lineage are known? We frame these explanations as three interacting processes: the assembly of regional species pools by dispersal, diversification and geographical restriction; environmental filtering of where species of those lineages occur; and the interaction strategy itself, which may in turn shape a lineage's niche and spread. Our tests are of pattern. We distinguish observed patterns, statistical associations, proposed processes and supported mechanisms; none of our results reaches the last. Table 1 sets out each explanation, the pattern it predicts, how we tested it, what we found and at which of these levels the result stands.

# Methods

## Strategies, occurrences and regions

We used the interaction types, taxonomy and cleaned occurrence records of a companion compilation of lycaenid–ant interactions (in preparation). Each species unit was classified as non-associated, facultative, obligate mutualist or obligate parasite, and the evidence for each type was recorded: either for the species itself, or presumed by the sources from relatives or from the genus. Riodinidae were not included. Of the `r format(n_units, big.mark = ",")` species units with occurrence records (`r format(n_records, big.mark = ",")` unique cleaned coordinates), `r format(n_class, big.mark = ",")` were classified: `r n_type("n")` non-associated, `r n_type("f")` facultative, `r n_type("m")` obligate mutualist and `r n_type("p")` obligate parasite. We assigned each species to the biogeographic region holding most of its records, using the realms of RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017 (Dinerstein et al., 2017) with Africa south of 15° S and Australia south of 10° S separated, giving eight regions. Assemblages were built in ISEA hexagons of about 23,000, 70,000 and 210,000 km² (Sahr et al., 2003) and mapped in the Equal Earth projection chosen with `crstools` (Pozzi et al., 2026). Classification is uneven: `r pct(ecomp("Australia"))` of the recorded species of Australia and `r pct(ecomp("Southern Africa"))` of southern Africa are classified, against `r pct(ecomp("Neotropic"))` of the Neotropics (Fig. 1f). To check that the regional contrasts do not follow from this unevenness, we recomputed the obligate share of each region with species-specific evidence only, in well-classified hexagons only, and with unclassified species imputed from their congeners, and related the GBIF records of each species to obligacy (Appendix S1).

## Environment and ants

Each species was described by the median over the 10-arc-minute pixels holding its records (sources in Table S1.2). Present climate came from WorldClim 2.1 (Fick & Hijmans, 2017): annual mean temperature, minimum temperature of the coldest month, precipitation seasonality, the precipitation of the driest month and an aridity index (precipitation over Hargreaves potential evapotranspiration; Hargreaves & Samani, 1985). Because seasonality measures how uneven rainfall is, not how long the dry season lasts, we also counted dry months (precipitation in mm below twice the mean temperature in °C), the longest run of dry months, and months of water deficit (precipitation below potential evapotranspiration). The change in temperature and precipitation since the LGM (21 ka) and the velocity of the temperature change (Sandel et al., 2011) came from Krapp et al. (2021), via `pastclim` (Leonardi et al., 2023); soil properties from SoilGrids 2.0 (Poggio et al., 2021) and He et al. (2021); the burned fraction of 2001–2020 from GFED5 (Chen et al., 2023); and the mean precipitation and share of dry time over the last 5 Myr from PALEO-PGEM (Barreto et al., 2023). For ants, each species was given the ant species richness estimated by Kass et al. (2022) over its records, and we counted, in each region, the species of the ant genera recorded with obligate lycaenids in the Global Ant Biodiversity Informatics records compiled by Kass et al. (2022), and the lycaenid species of each strategy recorded with them. Because presence in a region says little about local abundance, we also used the `r format(nrow(loc27), big.mark = ",")` sampled local ant communities of the Global Ant Database (Gibb et al., 2017): for each locality, the share of its species in *Crematogaster* or *Camponotus*, the two genera recorded with most obligate lycaenids, and its dominance, the share of its individuals in the most abundant species (only in localities where individuals were counted). We compared these among regions, adjusted dominance for the numbers of species and individuals sampled, and related them to the obligate share of hexagons of about 210,000 km² (quasi-binomial regressions, without and with region). Finally, we took colony size (workers in mature colonies), queen number and supercoloniality from the ant trait database of Bell-Roberts et al. (2024) and compared the partner species of obligate and facultative lycaenids (with random intercepts of ant genus), the median colony size of each partner genus with the obligate share of its lycaenid partners, and the obligacy of lycaenid species with the colony size of their partners.

## Climate and lineage out of sample

We analysed three nested contrasts: ant-associated against non-associated species, obligate (mutualist or parasite) against facultative species, and parasites against mutualists. For each, binomial models related the strategy to six predictors of present and past climate (annual mean temperature, aridity, precipitation seasonality, the LGM temperature and precipitation anomalies, and the temperature velocity), to lineage (random intercepts of subfamily and genus; `mgcv`, Wood, 2011), or to both. Because in-sample deviance explained measures description rather than generality, we judged the models by their predictions for species left out of the fit. We held out species (ten folds; their congeners remained in the training data), whole genera, whole subfamilies, and whole realms: each of the eight regions was predicted from the other seven. Against a baseline that predicts the share of the outcome in the training data, we compared climate, latitude interacting with hemisphere, lineage, and lineage with climate. For a genus or subfamily absent from the training data, the lineage models averaged the predicted probability over the estimated distribution of genus (and subfamily) effects, rather than giving it the effect of a typical lineage. So that a poor climate model would not merely reflect linear terms, we also fitted climate as a smooth term of each predictor (four basis functions) with a smooth interaction of temperature and aridity. For each held-out unit we report the predicted and observed share of the outcome, the area under the ROC curve (AUC, discrimination within the unit) and the deviance explained relative to the baseline, with 95% intervals from resampling genera within the unit. A held-out species was climatically novel when its Mahalanobis distance from the training species in the six climate predictors exceeded the 99th percentile of the training species' own distances. We repeated all schemes with species-specific evidence only.

## Comparisons within overlapping climates

We compared the five Mediterranean-climate regions, defined as Köppen–Geiger class Cs (Beck et al., 2023): the Cape, southern Australia, the Mediterranean Basin, California and central Chile. Because their climates are similar but not identical, we compared two regions only within the climate strata that both occupy, a coarsened exact matching (Iacus et al., 2012): strata of 2 °C annual mean temperature, 3 °C minimum temperature, 0.15 log10 aridity index and 15% precipitation seasonality, each occupied by at least five pixels of each region. Restricting two regions to common climatic support does not give them the same distribution over it. We therefore estimated the share of each strategy within each shared stratum and averaged it over common stratum weights, the mean of the two regions' area shares (or equal weights), using the strata in which both regions had at least three classified species. The quantity estimated is the composition of the species assemblage of the shared climates: a species recorded in several strata counted in each, so widespread species weighed more. In a second version, each species counted only in the shared stratum holding most of its records; in a third, each genus counted once in each region and stratum, so that the contrast compared genera rather than species. Intervals came from resampling genera (1,000 replicates), which keeps congeners and species of several strata together. We report the climatic balance of the regions before and after weighting, the share of each region's area and species retained, and the contrast for strata half as wide to twice as wide, for minimum occupancies of one to ten pixels and with species-specific evidence only. We then compared every pair of the eight biogeographic regions in the same way, within the climate strata they share across all their land (pairs with at least five shared strata); the pairs not involving southern Africa or Australia showed how much regions differ in shared climates. To describe how each fauna reaches its obligate share, we decomposed it into the share of species in genera that hold obligate species and the obligate share within those genera, and compared the share expected from each region's genera with a null in which the obligate shares of genera (over all their classified species) were permuted among the genera of each subfamily (999 permutations).

## Spread of genera

For each genus with a stem age on the dated tree of Yumnam & Kodandaramaiah (2025) and at least two recorded species, we counted the hexagons of about 210,000 km² holding its records and the biogeographic regions to which its species are assigned. A genus was obligate when at least half of its classified species were. We related the log number of hexagons and the number of regions beyond the first to obligacy, the log stem age and the log number of recorded species, with and without the genus's main region, and in phylogenetic regressions on a tree of genera (`phylolm`; Ho & Ané, 2014; Ives & Garland, 2010). Among associated species, we also compared the range areas of obligate and facultative species given region and lineage. We refitted the hexagon model with other definitions of an obligate genus (any obligate species; three quarters or all of the classified species obligate; the obligate share, also redrawn from a Beta distribution given the classified species and combined by Rubin's rules), with well-classified genera only, at two other grains, given the occurrence records of the genus, given subfamily or the spread of the rest of the subfamily, and within subfamilies, and compared each obligate genus with the non-obligate genera of its sister clade on the tree of genera. We also compared each maximal clade of obligate genera with its sister clade, on the tree of genera and on a tree of genera from Kawahara et al. (2023), for the hexagons, regions and landmasses of the glacial shelf occupied (given recorded species and stem age), range fragmentation, and climatic breadth relative to the climates available.

## What remains once region and lineage are known

For obligacy, we predicted each held-out subfamily with logistic regressions on geography (region, or latitude interacting with hemisphere), on geography with one environmental property added, and on each property alone. We estimated the effect of each property given region (a fixed effect) and lineage (random intercepts of subfamily and genus), for obligacy, for obligate mutualism against facultative species and for parasitism against mutualism, and adjusted the p-values for obligacy by the Holm method across all `r nrow(holm19)` properties. For results without a detectable effect, we report the 95% interval, which bounds the effects compatible with the data. Within the genera containing both outcomes of a contrast, we estimated the within-genus effect of each seasonality and drought property by conditional logistic regression on genus (R package `survival`), and compared the slope of a logistic regression with genus as a fixed effect with 9,999 permutations of the property among the species of each genus. For dry months, the clearest of these associations, we left out each genus with obligate species in turn, weighted every mixed genus equally, used water-deficit months instead, and fitted phylogenetic logistic regressions (Ives & Garland, 2010). We also split each species' dry months into those available, the mean over all land in the hexagons of about 210,000 km² holding its records, and its use beyond them, the difference between its own value and that mean, and did the same for temperature, annual and driest-month precipitation, elevation, net primary productivity and the cover of trees, shrubs, herbaceous and cultivated vegetation (1-km consensus land cover of Tuanmu & Jetz, 2014, averaged to 10 arc-minutes), each alone and together with dry months. Because hexagons defined by a species' own records make its baseline partly circular, we also compared the water availability used and accessible within 250 or 500 km of the records, and fitted presence–background models against the GBIF records of all butterflies (a target-group background; Phillips et al., 2009; Barber et al., 2022), with eligibility and outcomes set in advance (Appendix S5). Finally, to separate dryness from warmth, we compared the occupied pixels of obligate mutualists and their facultative relatives directly (a case–case comparison) within each contrast, one for each origin of obligate mutualism, using three variables fixed in advance: annual mean temperature (warmth), the longest run of months with less than 50 mm of rain (dry-season length, independent of temperature) and the annual climatic water deficit (water stress). We first checked that dryness varied within 1 °C temperature bins in every contrast. A species' score was the mean difference between its pixels and the other pixels of the same temperature bin (for warmth, of the same dry-season length), with every species weighted equally; scores were compared within contrasts and pooled over origins by random-effects meta-analysis (`metafor`; Viechtbauer, 2010), and the comparison was repeated within temperature bins and biomes. We related the same three variables to the four strategies as nested contrasts (any association, obligacy, mutualism against facultative association, parasitism against mutualism), given region and lineage and within genera.

## Origins of obligacy

We counted the origins of obligacy in 100 stochastic character maps (Huelsenbeck et al., 2003; Bollback, 2006; `phytools`, Revell, 2012) on the dated tree of Yumnam & Kodandaramaiah (2025) and the tree of Schär et al. (2018), pruned to their matched species or with missing species grafted to their genus, and on a tree of genera; each origin was assigned to the region holding most of its obligate descendants, and we tested whether gains and losses depend on hemisphere (Pagel, 1994). Because a region with more lineage history offers more opportunities for obligacy to arise, we also overlaid each map of obligacy on an independent map of three region groups and divided the gains in each group by the time its lineages spent non-obligate, comparing the southern rate with that elsewhere against gains placed at random along the non-obligate history; besides the trees above, we used trees of genera from the dated phylogeny of Kawahara et al. (2023). Because these estimates depend on the tree and on how unsampled species are placed, we treat them as exploratory.

# Results

## The strategies are structured in space and rest on few genera

Obligate mutualists were concentrated in southern Africa and Australia, obligate parasites in southern Africa, and non-associated species in the Holarctic (Fig. 1). The regions differed less in how many of their species were associated with ants, from `r pct(min(assoc_share$share))` in the `r assoc_share$region[which.min(assoc_share$share)]` to `r pct(max(assoc_share$share))` in `r south(assoc_share$region[which.max(assoc_share$share)])`, than in how they were associated (Appendix S1). Southern Africa held `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "p")` obligate parasites in `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "p", "genera")` genera and `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "m")` obligate mutualists in `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "m", "genera")` genera, and Australia `r lin_n("Australia", "m")` obligate mutualists in `r lin_n("Australia", "m", "genera")` genera. Obligate associates belonged to `r obligate_genera_total` genera worldwide, and none of the `r lin_n("Nearctic", "n") + lin_n("Nearctic", "f") + lin_n("Neotropic", "n") + lin_n("Neotropic", "f")` classified species of the Americas was obligate.

```{r fig1, fig.cap = "Global distribution of the ant-interaction strategies of lycaenid butterflies, in ISEA hexagons of about 210,000 km² (Equal Earth projection). (a–d) Proportions of classified species that were non-associated, facultative, obligate mutualists and obligate parasites, in hexagons with at least ten classified species. Each panel has its own square-root colour scale, spanning the 1st to 99th percentiles of its hexagons, so colours are not comparable between panels; hexagons beyond this range take the end colour (≤ or ≥ in the legend). (e) Classified species per hexagon (logarithmic scale). (f) Share of the recorded species of each hexagon that is classified, in hexagons with at least ten recorded species. Grey land has no estimate; colours are on one palette from light (low) to dark (high)."}
fig(d16, "plot_world_strategies.png")
```

This ordering did not follow from uneven knowledge (Appendix S1): with species-specific evidence only, obligate associates made up `r pct(kr("Southern Africa", "Species-specific evidence only"))` of the species of southern Africa and `r pct(kr("Australia", "Species-specific evidence only"))` of Australia, against at most `r pct(max(kspec[!region %in% c("Southern Africa", "Australia")]$obligate_share))` elsewhere, imputing unclassified species from their congeners changed no region but `r south(kimp[which.min(change)]$region)` by more than `r pts(max(abs(kimp[-which.min(change)]$change)))` points, and obligate species had `r pct(1 - 10^smp26$estimate)` fewer GBIF records than facultative species of the same region and lineage (`r pval(smp26$p)`).

## Similar climates hold different interactions

Within the `r std(cb, "strata")` climate strata shared by the Cape and the Mediterranean Basin, standardised to the same distribution over the strata, `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_1"))` of the Cape's classified species and `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_2"))` of the Basin's were obligate associates, a difference of `r pts(std(cb, "difference"))` percentage points (95% interval `r pts(std(cb, "difference_low"))`–`r pts(std(cb, "difference_high"))`; Fig. 2b). Both obligate strategies contributed: obligate mutualists made up `r pct(sh18(cb, "Cape", "m"))` of the Cape's species and `r pct(sh18(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "m"))` of the Basin's, and obligate parasites `r pct(sh18(cb, "Cape", "p"))` and `r pct(sh18(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "p"))`. The contrast held under every variant of the comparison (Fig. 2c): it was `r pts(std(cb, "difference", wt = "equal weights"))` points with equal stratum weights, `r pts(std(cb, "difference", ver = "main stratum of each species"))` points when each species counted only in its main stratum, `r pts(ssp(cb, "difference"))` points with species-specific evidence only, and between `r pts(min(sens18[pair == cb]$difference))` and `r pts(max(sens18[pair == cb]$difference))` points for every width of the strata and minimum occupancy, with lower 95% bounds of at least `r pts(min(sens18[pair == cb]$difference_low))` points.

Weighting each genus once per region and stratum, the Cape still differed from the Basin by `r pts(std(cb, "difference", ver = "genus-weighted"))` points (`r pts(std(cb, "difference_low", ver = "genus-weighted"))`–`r pts(std(cb, "difference_high", ver = "genus-weighted"))`): within shared climates, part of its excess came from holding more obligate genera, and the rest from the richness of these genera in species, the three largest holding `r pct(gwv("Cape", "top3_obligate_share"))` of the Cape's obligate species. Southern Australia differed from the Basin by `r pts(std(ab, "difference"))` points (`r pts(std(ab, "difference_low"))`–`r pts(std(ab, "difference_high"))`), a difference of similar size in every variant but with lower bounds close to zero, so the evidence for it is weaker than for the Cape. It came from many obligate genera with few species each (`r pts(std(ab, "difference", ver = "genus-weighted"))` points with genus weights) and was carried by obligate mutualists (`r pct(sh18(ab, "Southern Australia", "m"))` against `r pct(sh18(ab, "Mediterranean Basin", "m"))`). With genus weights, the Cape and southern Australia did not differ (`r pts(std("Cape vs Southern Australia", "difference", ver = "genus-weighted"))` points). None of the obligate species of the Cape or southern Australia belonged to a genus that also occurred in the Basin or California; the genera they shared, such as *Leptotes* and *Lycaena*, were represented only by facultative or non-associated species. California shared no climate stratum with the Cape or southern Australia (Appendix S4).

The two southern regions are obligate-rich in different ways (Appendix S4). In the climates shared with the Basin, `r pct(d43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Cape", "genera_with_obligate"))` of the Cape's genera held obligate species; these genera were almost entirely obligate (`r pct(d43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Cape", "W"))` of their species), rich in species and narrowly distributed (a median of `r num(d43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Cape", "median_hexagons_obligate_genera"), 0)` hexagons worldwide), and more than half of their obligate species were parasites. In southern Australia, `r pct(d43f("Shared climates: Southern Australia vs Mediterranean Basin", "Southern Australia", "genera_with_obligate"))` of genera held obligate species, `r pct(d43f("Shared climates: Southern Australia vs Mediterranean Basin", "Southern Australia", "W"))` of their species were obligate, almost all mutualists, and the genera were more widespread (median `r num(d43f("Shared climates: Southern Australia vs Mediterranean Basin", "Southern Australia", "median_hexagons_obligate_genera"), 0)` hexagons). Both held more obligate species than expected from their genera if obligacy were distributed among the genera of each subfamily at random (Cape `r pct(n43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Cape", "share"))` against a null median of `r pct(n43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Cape", "null_median"))`, `r pval(n43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Cape", "p_above"))`; southern Australia `r pct(n43f("Shared climates: Southern Australia vs Mediterranean Basin", "Southern Australia", "share"))` against `r pct(n43f("Shared climates: Southern Australia vs Mediterranean Basin", "Southern Australia", "null_median"))`, `r pval(n43f("Shared climates: Southern Australia vs Mediterranean Basin", "Southern Australia", "p_above"))`), as did southern Africa and Australia as wholes, whereas the Basin did not (`r pval(n43f("Shared climates: Cape vs Mediterranean Basin", "Mediterranean Basin", "p_above"))`).

(b) Share of each strategy among the classified species of the Cape or southern Australia (filled) and the Mediterranean Basin (open) within the climate strata each pair shares, standardised to a common distribution over the strata (area weights), with 95% intervals from resampling genera. (c) Difference in the obligate share between the regions of each pair under every variant of the comparison: the main analysis; equal stratum weights; each species counted only in its main stratum; each genus weighted once per region and stratum; species-specific evidence only; and (grey) strata half as wide to twice as wide with minimum occupancies of one to ten pixels. (d) Difference in the obligate share between southern Africa or Australia and each other biogeographic region within the climate strata they share across all their land (pairs with at least five shared strata), with 95% intervals from resampling genera; grey band: range of the differences between the pairs of other regions."}

```

Matching balanced the climates of the Cape and the Basin (standardised mean differences of temperature, aridity and seasonality at most `r num(max(abs(bal18[pair == cb & variable != "bio06"]$smd_after)))` after weighting, from up to `r num(max(abs(bal18[pair == cb & variable != "bio06"]$smd_before)))`; minimum temperature remained higher in the Cape) but covered only `r pct(rt(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "share_pixels"))` of the Basin's Mediterranean-climate pixels and `r pct(rt(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "share_species"))` of its classified species, against `r pct(rt(cb, "Cape", "share_pixels"))` and `r pct(rt(cb, "Cape", "share_species"))` of the Cape's (Appendix S4).

The southern excess was not particular to the Mediterranean-climate regions (Fig. 2a, d). Compared within the climate strata they share across all their land, southern Africa held more obligate species than `r aps("Southern Africa vs other regions", "intervals_above_zero")` of the `r aps("Southern Africa vs other regions", "pairs")` other regions with at least five shared strata, and Australia than `r aps("Australia vs other regions", "intervals_above_zero")` of `r aps("Australia vs other regions", "pairs")`, by medians of `r pts(aps("Southern Africa vs other regions", "median_difference"))` and `r pts(aps("Australia vs other regions", "median_difference"))` points; the intervals included zero only for `r ap_ns`. Southern Africa and Australia did not differ from each other (`r pts(ap24[pair == "Southern Africa vs Australia"]$difference)` points, `r pts(ap24[pair == "Southern Africa vs Australia"]$difference_low)` to `r pts(ap24[pair == "Southern Africa vs Australia"]$difference_high)`). The `r aps("Control pairs", "pairs")` pairs of the other regions differed by a median of `r pts(aps("Control pairs", "median_abs_difference"))` points; the largest differences, of up to `r pts(max(abs(c(aps("Control pairs", "min_difference"), aps("Control pairs", "max_difference")))))` points, separated the Neotropics, which hold no obligate species, from Indomalaya and New Guinea.

## Lineage predicts strategies while the genus is known; the climate models tested perform poorly

In sample, lineage described `r pct(ps("associated", "lineage"))` of the deviance in ant association, `r pct(ps("obligate", "lineage"))` in obligacy and `r pct(ps("parasite", "lineage"))` in parasitism against mutualism, and climate `r pct(ps("associated", "climate"))`, `r pct(ps("obligate", "climate"))` and `r pct(ps("parasite", "climate"))`, almost all of it shared with lineage; only `r ps("obligate", "mixed_genera")` genera contained both obligate and facultative species. Out of sample, knowing a species' genus still predicted its strategy (Fig. 3c): for held-out species, lineage explained `r pct(oos("associated", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))`, `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))` and `r pct(oos("parasite", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))` of the deviance in the three contrasts, and climate at most `r pct(max(oos_t[scheme == "species held out" & model == "climate" & evidence == "all"]$d2))`. With species-specific evidence only, lineage still explained `r pct(oos("associated", "specific", "species held out", "lineage"))`–`r pct(oos("obligate", "specific", "species held out", "lineage"))`, so the types presumed from relatives inflated the lineage signal only slightly (Appendix S2). The prediction rested on knowing the genus: for held-out genera, of which the model knew only the subfamily, lineage explained `r pct(oos("associated", "all", "genera held out", "lineage"))`, `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "genera held out", "lineage"))` and `r pct(oos("parasite", "all", "genera held out", "lineage"))` of the deviance, and climate `r pct(oos("associated", "all", "genera held out", "climate"))`, `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "genera held out", "climate"))` and `r pct(oos("parasite", "all", "genera held out", "climate"))`.

```{r fig3, out.width = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "100%" else "5.6in", fig.cap = "Lineage and climate as predictors of obligacy, and the spread of obligate genera. (a) Obligate share among the associated species of each realm (black bar) and as predicted by models fitted to the other seven realms (points, with 95% intervals from resampling genera within the realm). (b) Hexagons of about 210,000 km² holding the records of each obligate genus (at least half of its classified species obligate) and other genus, adjusted to the mean stem age and number of recorded species (points: genera; black: predicted hexagons with 95% intervals). (c) Deviance explained for the obligacy of associated species by lineage (random intercepts of subfamily and genus; an unseen genus or subfamily is averaged over the distribution of lineages), by climate (six predictors; for held-out subfamilies also as smooth terms with a temperature–aridity interaction) and by latitude and hemisphere: for species held out (their congeners stay in the training data), whole genera held out, whole realms held out, split into species whose genus also occurs in another realm and species of genera found only in the held-out realm, and whole subfamilies held out. Species and genera: median and range of three repeats of ten folds; realms and subfamilies: all held-out species pooled, relative to the share in the training data, with 95% intervals from resampling genera."}
fig(d22, "figure_3_lineage_climate.png")
```

The same held for whole realms (Fig. 3a, c). When each realm was predicted from the other seven, lineage explained `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage"))` of the deviance in obligacy (95% interval `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage", "d2_low"))`–`r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage", "d2_high"))`; AUC within realms `r num(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage", "auc"))`), latitude and hemisphere `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "latitude x hemisphere"))` (AUC `r num(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "latitude x hemisphere", "auc"))`), and climate `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate"))` (AUC `r num(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate", "auc"))`). Climate forecast that `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Neotropic", "climate"))` of the associated species of the Neotropics and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Palearctic", "climate"))` of the Palaearctic would be obligate, against `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Neotropic", "climate", "observed"))` and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Palearctic", "climate", "observed"), 0)` observed, and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Southern Africa", "climate"))` of those of southern Africa, against `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Southern Africa", "climate", "observed"))`. These failures were not extrapolations: at most `r pct(novel_max)` of the species of any held-out realm lay outside the climates of the training species. Flexible climate models did no better, explaining `r pct(fc("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate (flexible)"))` of the deviance in held-out realms (`r pct(fc("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate (flexible)", "d2_low"))` to `r pct(fc("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate (flexible)", "d2_high"))`) and `r pct(fc("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "climate (flexible)"))` in held-out subfamilies, and species-specific evidence did not change the comparison (Appendix S2). Lineage, too, missed the share of obligate species in realms whose genera it had not seen: it predicted `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Neotropic", "lineage"))` for the Neotropics, most of whose genera it had not seen and so gave the average of all genera, and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Australia", "lineage"))` for Australia, where obligate genera are endemic (`r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Australia", "lineage", "observed"))` observed), whereas latitude and hemisphere predicted `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Australia", "latitude x hemisphere"))`. Its advantage came from genera shared between realms: it explained `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus known", "lineage"))` of the deviance in obligacy for the `r bg("obligate", "genus known", "lineage", "species")` species whose genus also occurred in the training realms (AUC `r num(bg("obligate", "genus known", "lineage", "auc"))`), but `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "lineage"))` for the `r bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "lineage", "species")` species of genera found only in the held-out realm, where latitude and hemisphere explained `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "latitude x hemisphere"))` and climate `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "climate"))` (Appendix S2). For ant association and parasitism, climate and geography explained nothing in held-out realms (Appendix S2). For held-out subfamilies, which lineage could only average over (`r pct(po("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "lineage"))`), obligacy was the only contrast that climate (`r pct(po("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "climate"))`) or latitude and hemisphere (`r pct(po("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "latitude x hemisphere"))`) predicted.

Obligate genera were more confined than other genera (Fig. 3b; Appendix S6). At a given stem age and number of recorded species, obligate genera occupied `r num(exp(-spm("Hexagons occupied (log)")), 1)` times fewer hexagons (`r pval(spm("Hexagons occupied (log)", "p"))`), `r num(exp(-spm("Hexagons occupied (log), phylogenetic")), 1)` times fewer in phylogenetic regression on the tree of genera (`r pval(spm("Hexagons occupied (log), phylogenetic", "p"))`), and reached fewer regions beyond the first (`r pval(spm("Regions beyond the first (Poisson)", "p"))`), although they were not detectably more often confined to a single region (`r pval(spm("Confined to one region (logistic)", "p"))`). The association held, at `r num(min(cr33_main$ratio), 1)`–`r num(max(cr33_main$ratio), 1)` times fewer hexagons (all p ≤ `r num(max(cr33_main$p), 3)`), for other definitions of an obligate genus, for well-classified genera only, at grains three times finer and coarser, given the occurrence records of each genus, and given subfamily or the spread of the rest of the subfamily. It was weaker within Theclinae (`r num(crf("Within Theclinae"), 1)` times, `r pval(crf("Within Theclinae", "p"))`) and when each genus's obligate share was redrawn to carry its uncertain classification (`r num(crf("Obligate share, redrawn for incomplete classification"), 1)` times, `r pval(crf("Obligate share, redrawn for incomplete classification", "p"))`), and among close relatives it was not clear: in `r ss33$negative` of `r ss33$contrasts` contrasts with their sister clades on the tree of genera, obligate genera occupied fewer places (sign test `r pval(ss33$sign_test_p)`). Across the `r ct44[tree == "Tree of genera" & response == "hexagons_resid"]$contrasts` independent clades of obligate genera on each of two trees of genera, the obligate clade occupied fewer hexagons than its sister clade, given recorded species and stem age, in `r ct44[tree == "Tree of genera" & response == "hexagons_resid"]$obligate_lower` and `r ct44[tree == "Tree of genera (Kawahara)" & response == "hexagons_resid"]$obligate_lower` contrasts, and had a narrower temperature range than available in `r ct44[tree == "Tree of genera" & response == "temp_breadth"]$obligate_lower` and `r ct44[tree == "Tree of genera (Kawahara)" & response == "temp_breadth"]$obligate_lower`, but none of these differences was significant (Appendix S6). Of the `r nrow(ogr23)` obligate genera recorded in more than one region, `r ogr23[regions == 2, .N]` occurred in only two, such as *Lepidochrysops* in southern and tropical Africa and *Hypochrysops* in Australia and New Guinea. Within regions, climate gradients in composition arose mostly from the turnover of genera: of the `r nrow(gb)` gradients steeper than 0.3 log odds per SD, the composition expected from the genera present reproduced a median `r pct(median(gb$expected_slope / gb$observed_slope))` (Appendix S3).

## What remains: a southern geography of obligacy

Obligacy was the one contrast with a geography that crossed lineages. Latitude and hemisphere predicted the obligacy of held-out subfamilies (deviance explained `r num(sc("latitude x hemisphere", "subfamily"))`; Fig. 4a), better than the LGM temperature anomaly, which described the same concentration of obligate associates at southern mid-latitudes because the climate changed little there (alone, `r num(sc("anomaly", "subfamily"))`). Added to latitude and hemisphere, the anomaly did not improve the prediction (`r num(sc("latitude x hemisphere + anomaly", "subfamily"))`), and no soil property (including phosphorus), burned fraction, aridity or 5-Myr precipitation raised it by more than `r num(100 * max(dgain[scheme == "subfamily"]$gain), 1)` percentage points. Given region and lineage, the anomaly had no detectable effect (`r num(se("All associated species"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(se("All associated species", "p"))`), also in each hemisphere, without southern Africa, within genera and with species-specific evidence only (Appendix S5). This test is weak, however: its 95% interval (`r num(se("All associated species") - 1.96 * se("All associated species", "se"))` to `r num(se("All associated species") + 1.96 * se("All associated species", "se"))`) leaves effects of up to `r num(exp(1.96 * se("All associated species", "se") + abs(se("All associated species"))), 1)`-fold odds per SD compatible with the data.

```{r fig4, out.width = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "100%" else "6.5in", fig.cap = "What remains once region and lineage are known. (a) Deviance explained when the obligacy of the species of each subfamily is predicted by a logistic regression fitted to the other subfamilies: geography (latitude by hemisphere, dashed line; region), geography with one property added, and each property alone. (b) For every origin of obligate mutualism, the difference between its obligate mutualists and their facultative relatives in the longest run of months with less than 50 mm of rain at their occupied places (SD units, species weighted equally, 95% intervals): unmatched (grey), compared within 1 °C temperature bins (orange), and within temperature bins and biomes (black); diamonds: random-effects estimates over origins; in brackets: mutualist/facultative species. (c) The pooled estimates for annual mean temperature (H1, compared at the same dry-season length), the run of months below 50 mm (H2) and the climatic water deficit (H3), at each level of matching."}
fig(d22, "figure_4_remaining_signal.png")
```

Given region and lineage, obligate associates lived in drier climates than facultative species, an association carried by obligate mutualists (Appendix S5). The number of dry months had the largest effect (`r num(dr("obligate", "dry_months"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(dr("obligate", "dry_months", "p"))`; for obligate mutualists against facultative species `r num(dr("mutualist", "dry_months"))`), followed by the longest dry spell, which was almost the same measure (r = `r num(cor(spd19$dry_months, spd19$dry_run, use = "complete.obs"))`), the precipitation of the driest month (`r num(dr("obligate", "bio14"))`) and precipitation seasonality (`r num(dr("obligate", "bio15"))`). After Holm adjustment over the `r nrow(holm19)` properties tested, only the number of dry months remained below 0.05, narrowly (adjusted `r pval(hb("dry_months", "p_holm"))`); seasonality did not (adjusted `r pval(hb("bio15", "p_holm"))`). Parasites did not differ from mutualists in any of these properties (all p ≥ `r num(min(dr19[contrast == "parasite"]$p))`).

Within the `r nrow(mix19)` genera with both obligate and facultative species, the obligate species lived in climates with more dry months and more seasonal rainfall than their facultative congeners (conditional logistic regression, `r num(wg("obligate", "dry_months", "conditional_estimate"))` log odds per SD for dry months, `r pval(wg("obligate", "dry_months", "conditional_p"))`; `r num(wg("obligate", "bio15", "conditional_estimate"))` for seasonality, `r pval(wg("obligate", "bio15", "conditional_p"))`), beyond the range of 9,999 permutations among the species of each genus; the same held for obligate mutualists alone (`r num(wg("mutualist", "dry_months", "conditional_estimate"))` for dry months) but not for parasites against mutualists (`r pval(wg("parasite", "dry_months", "conditional_p"))`). The association rested on few genera, mostly Australian and Indomalayan Theclinae such as *Hypochrysops*, *Arhopala* and *Ogyris*: leaving out *Arhopala* alone weakened the effect of dry months on obligate mutualism given region and lineage to `r num(logo28[left_out == "Arhopala" & analysis == "Given region and lineage"]$estimate)` log odds per SD (`r pval(logo28[left_out == "Arhopala" & analysis == "Given region and lineage"]$p)`), and months of water deficit showed no association given region and lineage (`r pval(drb("obligate", "deficit_months", "Given region and lineage", "p"))`), although they did in phylogenetic logistic regressions (Appendix S5). Because `r carn19[strategy == "p"]$carnivorous` of the `r carn19[strategy == "p"]$carnivory_recorded` parasites with a recorded diet are carnivorous in ant nests, against `r carn19[strategy == "m"]$carnivorous` of `r carn19[strategy == "m"]$carnivory_recorded` mutualists, the association concerns larvae tended by ants rather than those that prey on them.

These associations describe where species live, not whether they occupy drier places than their relatives under the same conditions. Relative to their surroundings, obligate mutualists occupied places with more dry months than their facultative congeners in `r asf("mutualist", "beyond", "positive")` of `r asf("mutualist", "beyond", "genera")` mixed genera, and against a background of all butterfly records the difference was positive but uncertain (Appendix S5). Because dry months are defined by temperature, we turned to measures that are not: the run of months with less than 50 mm of rain and the water deficit varied within 1 °C temperature bins nearly as much as overall in every contrast (within-bin standard deviation `r pct(min(id38$sd_ratio))`–`r pct(max(id38$sd_ratio))` of the total), so a drought effect could have been detected at fixed temperature. Compared directly at the same temperature, the occupied places of obligate mutualists did not have detectably longer dry seasons than those of their facultative relatives (difference `r ci41(p41, "H2")` SD, positive in `r c41(p41, "H2", "positive")` of `r c41(p41, "H2", "origins")` origins; Fig. 4b, c) or a greater water deficit (`r ci41(p41, "H3")`), and at the same dry-season length they were not warmer (`r ci41(p41, "H1")`). Without matching, the dry-season difference was `r ci41(u41, "H2")`; matching on temperature reduced it, and matching on temperature and biome removed it (`r ci41(b41, "H2")`). Across the four strategies, any association and parasitism were unrelated to warmth, dry-season length and water stress, given region and lineage and within genera; obligate mutualism went with each of them alone, but within genera only warmth kept an effect when the three were entered together (`r num(s42f("mutualist", "Within genera", "bio01", mo = "Together"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(s42f("mutualist", "Within genera", "bio01", "p", mo = "Together"))`; Appendix S5). Adding GBIF records changed the estimates mainly by changing which species qualified, and a power simulation showed that more records per species would not help, whereas more species per origin or more origins would (Appendix S5).

Ant richness did not account for the geography of obligacy. Given region and lineage, the estimated ant species richness of a species' records had no detectable effect on obligacy (`r num(ar("obligate", "region and lineage"))` log odds per SD, 95% interval `r num(ar("obligate", "region and lineage") - 1.96 * ar("obligate", "region and lineage", "se"))` to `r num(ar("obligate", "region and lineage") + 1.96 * ar("obligate", "region and lineage", "se"))`, which excludes all but a weak positive effect) or parasitism (`r pval(ar("parasite", "region and lineage", "p"))`). Of the `r obl_partner` obligate species with recorded partners, `r obl_cc` were recorded with *Crematogaster* or *Camponotus*. Both genera occurred in the Cape, southern Australia, the Mediterranean Basin and California and were richest in the Basin (`r av("Crematogaster", "Mediterranean Basin")` *Crematogaster* and `r av("Camponotus", "Mediterranean Basin")` *Camponotus* species, against `r av("Crematogaster", "Cape")` and `r av("Camponotus", "Cape")` in the Cape), where `r av("Crematogaster", "Mediterranean Basin", "f")` and `r av("Camponotus", "Mediterranean Basin", "f")` facultative lycaenids were recorded with them (Appendix S5). The other partner genera of southern obligate species were mostly regional, such as *Iridomyrmex* and *Anonychomyrma* in Australia and *Anoplolepis* in southern Africa.

Nor were the two partner genera more prevalent in the local ant communities of obligate-rich regions (Appendix S5). They made up a median `r pct(rc("Southern Africa", "partner_species"))` of the ant species of a sampled locality in southern Africa and `r pct(rc("Australia", "partner_species"))` in Australia, against `r pct(rc("Palearctic", "partner_species"))` in the Palaearctic and `r pct(rc("Nearctic", "partner_species"))` in the Nearctic, and `r pct(rc("Mediterranean Basin", "partner_species"))` in the Mediterranean-climate Basin (`r rc("Mediterranean Basin", "localities")` localities) against `r pct(rc("Cape", "partner_species"))` in the Cape (`r rc("Cape", "localities")` localities); even at the limits of their intervals, the southern regions exceeded the Palaearctic and Nearctic by at most `r pts(max(rc("Southern Africa", "partner_species_high"), rc("Australia", "partner_species_high")) - min(rc("Palearctic", "partner_species_low"), rc("Nearctic", "partner_species_low")))` percentage points. Local communities were more dominated by their most abundant species in southern Africa and Australia (medians `r pct(rc("Southern Africa", "dominance"))` and `r pct(rc("Australia", "dominance"))`) than in the Palaearctic and Nearctic (`r pct(rc("Palearctic", "dominance"))` and `r pct(rc("Nearctic", "dominance"))`), but nearly as much in Indomalaya and New Guinea (`r pct(rc("Indomalayan", "dominance"))` and `r pct(rc("New Guinea and islands", "dominance"))`), where obligate associates are fewer. After accounting for the numbers of species and individuals sampled, only Australia remained more dominated than the Palaearctic (`r num(da27[region == "Australia"]$estimate)` on the logit scale, `r pval(da27[region == "Australia"]$p)`; southern Africa `r pval(da27[region == "Southern Africa"]$p)`). Within regions, hexagons whose sampled communities were more dominated held proportionally fewer obligate lycaenids (`r num(hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == TRUE]$estimate)` log odds per SD, `r pval(hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == TRUE]$p)`, `r hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == TRUE]$hexagons` hexagons), and the share of partner genera was unrelated to obligacy (`r pval(hm27[measure == "partner_species" & given_region == TRUE]$p)`).

Colony size, recorded for `r pa30[is.finite(colony_size), .N]` of the `r nrow(pa30)` partner ant species (Bell-Roberts et al., 2024), gave only weak evidence that obligate lycaenids use ants with larger colonies (Appendix S5). Within ant genera, the species recorded with obligate lycaenids had colonies about `r num(10^at30[grepl("^log10 colony size, obligate partners vs facultative only .genus RE", test)]$estimate, 1)` times as large as those recorded only with facultative ones (`r pval(at30[grepl("^log10 colony size, obligate partners vs facultative only .genus RE", test)]$p)`; `r pa30[is.finite(colony_size) & partner != "facultative only", .N]` and `r pa30[is.finite(colony_size) & partner == "facultative only", .N]` species), and they were not more often polygynous or supercolonial. Across partner genera, the median colony size of a genus was unrelated to the obligate share of its lycaenid partners (Spearman `r num(gt30[grepl("Spearman", test)]$estimate)`, `r pval(gt30[grepl("Spearman", test)]$p)`). Among lycaenid species, those whose partners belonged to species or genera with larger colonies were more often obligate mutualists, given region and lineage (`r num(ltf("mutualist", "partner_cs", "region and lineage"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(ltf("mutualist", "partner_cs", "region and lineage", "p"))`), but the partners of southern Africa's obligate species, mostly *Crematogaster* and *Camponotus*, had smaller typical colonies than those of its facultative species.

## Origins of obligacy

Obligacy arose repeatedly, but the number of origins in each region depended on the tree (Appendix S6): on the tree of genera, `r og_med("Southern Africa")` times in southern Africa (`r og_gen("Southern Africa")` obligate genera) and `r og_med("Australia")` times in Australia (`r og_gen("Australia")` genera), while the species trees added origins within genera, mainly in Australia and Indomalaya. Per million years of non-obligate lineage history, obligacy arose `r num(rr25(ts, "ratio_median"), 1)` times as often in southern Africa and Australia as elsewhere on the pruned Yumnam tree (95% range over maps `r num(rr25(ts, "ratio_low"), 1)`–`r num(rr25(ts, "ratio_high"), 1)`), `r num(rr25(tg, "ratio_median"), 1)` times on the tree of genera (`r num(rr25(tg, "ratio_low"), 1)`–`r num(rr25(tg, "ratio_high"), 1)`), and `r num(rr25(tk, "ratio_median"), 1)` times on a tree of genera from the phylogeny of Kawahara et al. (2023; `r num(rr25(tk, "ratio_low"), 1)`–`r num(rr25(tk, "ratio_high"), 1)`), which rests on different sequence data but the same strategies; with so few origins, however, this excess was not clearly beyond what gains placed at random along the non-obligate history produce (one-sided p = `r num(min(r25$p_null))` to `r num(max(r25$p_null))` across trees). Southern origins were older (median `r num(median(ga25[tree == tg & group == "South"]$age), 0)` Myr on the tree of genera) than those of the Holarctic and the Americas (`r num(median(ga25[tree == tg & group == "Holarctic and Americas"]$age), 0)` Myr).

# Discussion

Across the globe, the strategies of lycaenid butterflies followed their lineages more closely than their climates (Table 1). These are observations about pattern: they show that the geography of the strategies is better described by the composition of regional lineages than by climate, not why each region holds the lineages it does.

**What is new.** Pierce et al. (2002) attributed part of the southern excess of obligate associations to the composition of southern faunas; we tested this suggestion against climate directly. Within the climates the Cape shares with the Mediterranean Basin, the Cape holds far more obligate associates, both mutualists and parasites, and none of the southern obligate species belongs to a genus present in the Basin or California. The difference therefore lies in which lineages each region holds, not in how the same lineages behave under the same climate. The evidence is strongest for the Cape; for southern Australia the difference is of similar size but less certain. The comparison of every pair of regions places this contrast in a wider pattern: southern Africa and Australia hold more obligate species than nearly every region they share climates with, whereas the other regions differ by a median of a few points. The two southern regions reach their obligate richness differently: the Cape through a few obligate genera rich in species, among them *Chrysoritis*, *Thestor* and *Lepidochrysops*, and southern Australia through many obligate genera with few species each, almost all mutualists; weighted by genera, the two do not differ. Both hold more obligate species than their genera would carry if obligacy were spread among the genera of each subfamily at random, so the southern excess lies not in which subfamilies are present but in which of their genera reached and persisted in the south.

**The Americas.** None of the classified lycaenids of the Americas is obligate, although the climates of the obligate-rich south recur there. Only a few blue lineages reached the New World, through a Beringian gateway that filtered them by climate (Vila et al., 2011), and none of them is obligate. Much of the myrmecophily of Neotropical caterpillars belongs to the sister family Riodinidae, more than 90% of whose species are Neotropical (Espeland et al., 2015) and about a fifth of which are known or inferred to associate with ants (Pierce & Dankowicz, 2022). The absence of obligate lycaenids from the Americas thus concerns the lineages of one family; with only `r pct(ecomp("Neotropic"))` of its recorded lycaenids classified, the Neotropical fauna is also the least known (Fiedler, 2021).

**Ants.** Neither the richness of ants nor the presence or local prevalence of *Crematogaster* and *Camponotus*, the genera most often recorded with obligate species, accounts for the scarcity of obligate associates in the north, where these genera are rich in species and tend facultative lycaenids. Local communities in southern Africa and Australia were more dominated by single species, as expected if obligate associations need dominant ants with large, long-lived colonies (Fiedler, 2021), but so were those of Indomalaya and New Guinea, and within regions more dominated communities went with fewer obligate lycaenids. At the level of partner species, colony size gave only weak support: within ant genera, the partners of obligate lycaenids had somewhat larger colonies, but the database covers few partner species, mostly Holarctic ones, and the partners of southern Africa's obligate species do not stand out. The two ant results that point in opposite directions measure different things: colony size is a property of a partner species, whereas dominance describes how a local community is shared among all its species, so a species with large colonies can be a minor part of a diverse community and a species with small colonies can dominate one. Obligate mutualism may therefore go with particular compatible colonies rather than with numerically dominant ant communities, a hypothesis these data cannot test. Whether the partner species of the north offer the colonies that obligate larvae need remains open, and needs colony data for the southern partner species, above all in *Crematogaster*.

**The southern geography of obligacy.** Obligacy was the one strategy predicted in lineages the model had not seen, and the signal was geographic: obligate associates, in several subfamilies, are concentrated at southern mid-latitudes. The small glacial climate change of the southern continents described this concentration only because it is small there, and added nothing detectable once region and lineage were known, though that test could not exclude sizeable effects; glacial stability (Dynesius & Jansson, 2000; Sandel et al., 2011) cannot be separated from whatever else distinguishes the southern continents; soils, fire and ant richness did no better. These are tests of the variables we specified, not evidence that climate history had no influence. Obligate genera occupy fewer places than other genera of the same age and size, an association robust to how obligacy, classification, grain, sampling and clade are treated, but not clear among close relatives: across independent clades of obligate genera, the obligate clade was less widespread than its sister clade in most contrasts on both trees, but not significantly so. It is consistent with dependence on particular ants limiting how far lineages spread, which would keep obligacy that arose in one region there; but lineages with restricted ranges may equally become obligate more often, or both may follow from a shared history, and the data do not distinguish these, nor show that confinement produced the southern concentration. Obligacy may also have arisen more often in the south per unit of lineage history: the point estimates were higher there on every tree, but within the range expected by chance with so few origins. Old, infertile, climatically buffered landscapes, where carbohydrate-rich vegetation supports abundant, dominant ants (Orians & Milewski, 2007; Hopper, 2009), remain a plausible setting for southern obligate lineages, and the convergence of the Cape and Australia in seed dispersal by ants (Lengyel et al., 2010) suggests that such settings affect other ant interactions too. Our data describe where obligate lineages are rather than how they got there: the origins of obligacy we counted depend on the tree, and rates of diversification estimated from extant species alone cannot distinguish speciation from extinction (Rabosky & Benson, 2021).

**Dry seasons among close relatives.** Once region and lineage were known, obligate mutualists lived in warmer, more seasonally dry climates than facultative species, also among congeners, and in the drier parts of their surroundings. Compared at the same temperature, however, and above all within the same biome, their places were not detectably drier than those of their facultative relatives, although dryness varied enough at fixed temperature to have revealed a difference. The association is therefore better described as a difference in the habitats the two strategies occupy than as a response to drought itself. It agrees with the idea that larvae protected by ants survive dry seasons better (Cottrell, 1984; Espeland et al., 2023) only at the coarse scale of habitat, and that idea was proposed mainly for parasites, which showed no association at all. With few contrasts, most resting on one or two species of a strategy, the data cannot exclude a modest effect; a target-group background, which also carries the ecology of the recorded butterflies (Botella et al., 2020), does not resolve it either. More species per contrast, and more independent origins, would help more than more records; which mutualist larvae shelter in nests, when they develop relative to the dry season, and which host plants and habitats they use would test the idea directly.

**Conclusions.** Three findings are established: the interaction strategies differ markedly among regions with comparable climates, they are concentrated in lineages, and the southern faunas hold disproportionately the obligate genera of their subfamilies. Obligate genera are less widespread than other genera, an association whose cause is unresolved and which does not clearly replicate among sister clades. A drier niche of obligate mutualists appears at the scale of species ranges but not at matched temperature and habitat. Simple explanations based on total ant richness, the glacial climate anomaly, soils or fire are not supported by the proxies we used. Why obligacy evolved in a few southern lineages, and why they remained there, is unresolved; the larval natural history of related mutualists and facultative species, the colony traits of their partner ants and dated range histories of well-resolved clades are the evidence now needed.

# Data availability statement {-}

The interaction data, cleaned occurrence records, environmental layers and the R code of all analyses will be archived in a public repository (Zenodo) on acceptance; an anonymous link will be provided for review.

```{r si-setup, include=FALSE}
# Supporting figures are inserted as captioned images (numbered S1.1, S1.2, ... by hand, outside
# the numbering of the main figures); paths are relative to writing/
si_fig <- function(dir, file, caption) {
  cat("![", caption, "](", file.path("../data/intermediate", basename(dir), file),
      "){width=6.5in}\n\n", sep = "")
}
# Supporting tables: a bold caption paragraph, then the table
si_tab <- function(caption, tab) {
  cat("**", caption, "**\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(tab, align = ifelse(vapply(tab, is.numeric, logical(1)), "r", "l")))
  cat("\n\n")
}
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pv <- function(p) vapply(p, function(x) if (is.na(x)) "–" else pval(x), character(1))
f0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
ci <- function(est, lo, hi) ifelse(is.na(est), "–", paste0(pct(est), " (", pct(lo), "–", pct(hi), ")"))
cin <- function(est, lo, hi) paste0(f2(est), " (", f2(lo), " to ", f2(hi), ")")
contrast_names <- c(associated = "Associated vs non-associated", obligate = "Obligate vs facultative",
                    parasite = "Parasite vs mutualist", mutualist = "Mutualist vs facultative")
type_names <- c(n = "Non-associated", f = "Facultative", m = "Obligate mutualist",
                p = "Obligate parasite")
model_names <- c(baseline = "Baseline", climate = "Climate",
                 `latitude x hemisphere` = "Lat. × hem.", lineage = "Lineage",
                 `lineage + climate` = "Lineage + climate")
property_names <- c(lgm_anomaly_temperature = "LGM temperature anomaly", log_aridity = "Aridity",
                    bio15 = "Precipitation seasonality", dry_months = "Dry months",
                    dry_run = "Longest dry spell", bio14 = "Driest-month precipitation",
                    phh2o = "Soil pH", cec = "Soil cation exchange capacity",
                    nitrogen = "Soil nitrogen", soc = "Soil organic carbon",
                    soil_p = "Soil phosphorus", fire = "Burned fraction",
                    pgem_log_precipitation = "5-Myr mean precipitation",
                    pgem_dry_share = "5-Myr share of dry time")
pname <- function(v) ifelse(v %in% names(property_names), property_names[v], v)

## Appendix S1. Data: evidence, completeness and environmental layers {-}

The interaction types come from a companion compilation (in preparation). For each type, the sources either gave evidence for the species itself or presumed the type from relatives or from the genus. Table S1.1 gives, for each region, the recorded and classified species and the classified species of each strategy, with the share whose type was presumed from relatives. Figure S1.1 shows the same information with the out-of-sample prediction of Fig. 3c, repeated with species-specific evidence only. Table S1.2 lists the environmental, ant and phylogenetic data. Table S1.3 and Figure S1.2 test whether the regional obligate shares follow from uneven knowledge.

```{r tab-s1-1, results = "asis"}
cov <- ecov[, .(N = sum(N)), by = .(region, strategy, evidence, recorded, classified)]
cell <- function(rg, k) {
  x <- cov[region == rg & strategy == k]
  if (!nrow(x)) return("0")
  n <- sum(x$N)
  paste0(n, " (", pct(sum(x[evidence == "presumed from relatives"]$N) / n), ")")
}
reg_order <- c("Nearctic", "Neotropic", "Palearctic", "Tropical Africa", "Southern Africa",
               "Indomalayan", "Australia", "New Guinea and islands")
t1 <- rbindlist(lapply(reg_order, function(rg) {
  x <- unique(cov[region == rg, .(recorded, classified)])
  data.table(Region = rg, Recorded = x$recorded,
             Classified = paste0(x$classified, " (", pct(x$classified / x$recorded), ")"),
             `Non-assoc.` = cell(rg, "n"), Facultative = cell(rg, "f"),
             Mutualist = cell(rg, "m"), Parasite = cell(rg, "p"))
}))
si_tab("Table S1.1. Recorded and classified species of each region (in brackets: share of the recorded species that is classified), and the classified species of each strategy (in brackets: share whose type was presumed from relatives or from the genus by the sources). Species are assigned to the region holding most of their records.", t1)
```

```{r fig-s1-1, results = "asis"}

(B) Deviance explained by lineage, climate and both, in sample, for species held out (ten folds) and for whole genera held out, with all classified species (filled) and species-specific evidence only (open); medians of three repeats. (C) Prediction of the obligacy of held-out subfamilies and genera by region, latitude and hemisphere and the LGM temperature anomaly, with both evidence sets.")

## Appendix S2. Climate and lineage among species {-}

Table S2.1 partitions the in-sample deviance of each contrast between climate (six predictors) and lineage (random intercepts of subfamily and genus); Table S2.2 gives the same models for held-out species and genera. Tables S2.3 and S2.4 and Figure S2.1 give the predictions for held-out realms and subfamilies: pooled over all held-out species, and for each held-out unit, with calibration, discrimination and climatic novelty. Figure S2.2 shows the climate coefficients of phylogenetic logistic regressions (Ives & Garland, 2010) on the Yumnam and Schär trees. Table S2.5 splits the predictions for held-out realms by whether a species' genus also occurs in the training realms, and Table S2.6 compares linear and flexible climate models for held-out realms and subfamilies, with both evidence sets.

## Appendix S3. Composition within regions {-}

Within each region, we described the share of each strategy along temperature, aridity and the LGM anomaly in hexagons of about 210,000 km². To separate the turnover of lineages from change within lineages, each species was given the strategy composition of its congeners, itself excluded, and the mean over a hexagon's species gave the composition expected from the lineages present. We compared the part of each gradient that this expectation did not reproduce with 199 permutations of strategies among the species of each genus.

Within regions, composition changed along climate gradients, mostly through the turnover of genera. Of the `r nrow(gb)` gradients steeper than 0.3 log odds per SD, the composition expected from the genera present had the same sign in `r pct(mean(sign(gb$expected_slope) == sign(gb$observed_slope)))` and reproduced a median `r pct(median(gb$expected_slope / gb$observed_slope))` of the observed slope; the remainder exceeded the range of permutations of strategies within genera in only `r gnt$slopes_beyond_null` gradients. In Europe, for example, the share of non-associated species rose northwards because facultative richness per hexagon fell (by `r pct(-rs("Europe", "facultative_change_per_10deg"))` per 10° of latitude) as genera centred in the south, such as *Polyommatus*, *Lysandra* and *Leptotes*, thinned out; the share expected from the genera present rose almost as steeply as the observed share (`r num(shv("Europe", "latitude_z", "expected_slope"))` against `r num(shv("Europe", "latitude_z", "observed_slope"))` log odds per SD of latitude).

Figure S3.1 shows the share of each strategy along temperature, aridity and the LGM temperature anomaly within each region, observed and expected from the genera present. Table S3.1 tests whether the species-level relationships differ among regions. Figure S3.2 analyses ant association along latitude in Europe (hexagons of about 23,000 km²; species richness of each strategy modelled with quasi-Poisson regressions), and Figure S3.3 and Table S3.2 extend the analysis to the eastern Palaearctic and the Nearctic, and to temperature effects on association among species in every region.

Share of each strategy along annual mean temperature, aridity and the LGM temperature anomaly within regions (hexagons of about 210,000 km²). Solid: observed; dashed: expected from the lineages present (each species given the strategy composition of its congeners, itself excluded). Points are hexagons.")
```

The composition of the obligate faunas (Table S4.8, Figure S4.5) decomposes the obligate share of each biogeographic region, Mediterranean-climate region and climate-matched subset into the share of species in genera that hold obligate species (R) and the obligate share within those genera (W), and compares the share expected from each region's genera with a null in which the obligate shares of genera are permuted among the genera of each subfamily.

               p = pv(p_above))]

## Appendix S5. What remains once region and lineage are known {-}

Figure S5.1 and Table S5.1 test whether the obligacy signal reflects glacial stability. Figure S5.2 tests soils, fire and long-term aridity, and Table S5.2 gives the effect of every property on obligacy given region and lineage, with Holm-adjusted p-values. Figures S5.3 and S5.4 and Tables S5.3–S5.7 give the association of precipitation seasonality with obligacy under strong controls, the drought measures, every genus with both obligate and facultative species, the within-genus permutation tests and larval carnivory. Figure S5.5 and Table S5.8 give the ant analyses, and Figure S5.6 the permutation nulls. Table S5.9 and Figure S5.7 test the robustness of the association with dry months, and Table S5.10 and Figure S5.8 describe the local ant communities. Table S5.11 and Figure S5.9 separate the dry months available around each species from its use of drier places, Table S5.12 and Figure S5.10 show what the drier places of obligate mutualists are, Table S5.13 and Figure S5.11 compare water availability used and accessible with independently drawn accessible areas, Table S5.14 and Figure S5.12 relate adult flight months to the dry season, and Table S5.15 and Figure S5.13 give the colony traits of the partner ants. Tables S5.16–S5.18 and Figures S5.14–S5.16 give the first version of the test of the dry-season association against a background of all butterfly records, and Table S5.19 and Figure S5.17 its second version; Figures S5.18–S5.24 and Tables S5.20–S5.23 give the diagnostics, the matched comparison that Fig. 4b, c summarises, and the four strategies.

The first version of the presence–background test fitted inhomogeneous Poisson point-process models as infinitely weighted logistic regressions (Warton & Shepherd, 2010; Fithian & Hastie, 2013) within accessible areas defined as the realms on each landmass of the glacial shelf (Barve et al., 2011; land above −120 m in ETOPO1, NOAA National Geophysical Data Center, 2009), with spatially blocked cross-validation (Valavi et al., 2019); its per-genus estimates are shown in Figure S5.18. Before any further model, we checked whether drought could be told apart from warmth in each contrast (Table S5.20, Figure S5.19), audited the GBIF supplementation and the number of independent origins (Table S5.21, Figure S5.20) and simulated the power of possible data additions (Figure S5.21). The matched case–case comparison of mutualists and facultative relatives is in Table S5.22 and Figures S5.22–S5.23, and the four strategies against warmth, dry-season length and water stress in Table S5.23 and Figure S5.24. These analyses were designed after the earlier results were known and are sequential.

```

## Appendix S6. Spread and origins of obligate lineages {-}

Table S6.3 and Figure S6.2 relate the spread of genera to obligacy, and Table S6.4 lists the obligate genera recorded in more than one region. Table S6.5 and Figure S6.3 give the rates of origin of obligacy per unit of non-obligate lineage history in three groups of regions, and Table S6.6 and Figure S6.4 the robustness of the confinement of obligate genera. Table S6.1 tests whether gains and losses of obligacy depend on hemisphere (Pagel, 1994) on both trees, and Figure S6.1 shows the rates of the dependent model and the origins on the grafted Yumnam tree. Table S6.2 gives the origins of obligacy per region on all four trees. These counts depend on the tree and on the placement of unsampled species, and are exploratory.

                 Species = species, `logL independent` = f2(logL_independent),

si_tab("Table S6.1. Correlated evolution of obligacy and hemisphere (Pagel, 1994): likelihoods of the independent and dependent models on both genus-grafted trees, with polytomies resolved at random.", t22)
```

(B) Origins of obligacy in 100 stochastic character maps on the genus-grafted Yumnam tree, by the region of the obligate species descended from each origin; point size and position give the number of those species.")
